outputs.L1:
### From *An Evening’s Love*

Calm was the evening, and clear was the sky,  
And the newly budding flowers sprang,  
When Amyntas and I wandered all alone  
To hear the sweet nightingale sing.  
I sat, and he lay down beside me,  
But scarcely a breath could he draw;  
For when, with some fear, he began to draw near,  
He was dashed with “Ah, ha, ha, ha, ha!”

He blushed to himself and lay still for a while,  
As modesty curbed his desire;  
But soon, with a smile, I dispelled all his fears,  
Adding new flames to his fire.  
“O Silvia,” he said, “you are cruel  
To keep your poor lover in awe.”  
Then once more he pressed his hand to my breast,  
But was dashed with “Ah, ha, ha, ha, ha!”

I knew it was passion that caused all his fear,  
And therefore I pitied his case.  
I softly whispered, “There’s nobody near,”  
And laid my cheek close to his face.  
But just as he grew ever bolder,  
A shepherd passed by us and saw;  
And just as our bliss began with a kiss,  
He laughed out, “Ah, ha, ha, ha, ha!”
outputs.L2:
**From *An Evening’s Love***

The twilight rested peacefully beneath a cloudless sky,  
while newly opened blossoms rose from the earth.  
Amyntas and I wandered out alone  
to listen to the nightingale’s lovely song.

I took my seat, and he stretched out beside me,  
so nervous he could hardly breathe.  
When at last he timidly moved closer,  
I startled him by laughing, “Ha, ha, ha, ha!”

Embarrassed, he reddened and remained quiet for a time,  
his shyness restraining what he longed to do.  
Yet a smile from me soon put his worries to rest  
and made his desire burn even more fiercely.

“You are heartless, Silvia,” he said,  
“to leave your unhappy lover so afraid.”  
Again he reached out and pressed his hand against my breast,  
but I checked him with another “Ha, ha, ha, ha!”

I understood that strong feeling was the source of his fear,  
so I felt compassion for him.  
Softly I whispered that no one else was nearby  
and brought my cheek close against his face.

Just as his courage continued to grow,  
a passing shepherd noticed us.  
At the very moment our happiness began with a kiss,  
the shepherd burst into laughter: “Ha, ha, ha, ha!”
outputs.L3:
On a calm and peaceful evening, Amyntas and Silvia wander away together to listen to the nightingale’s song. Surrounded by the stillness of the countryside, they find themselves alone in an intimate setting. Amyntas longs to express his affection for Silvia, but fear and modesty initially hold him back, making his advances hesitant and restrained.

Silvia, however, gently encourages him. Through affectionate smiles, whispered words, and increasing physical closeness, she reassures Amyntas that his feelings are welcome. Her warmth gradually overcomes his uncertainty, strengthening both his confidence and his desire. At last, the two lovers move closer and begin to kiss.

Their private moment is short-lived. A shepherd passing nearby unexpectedly discovers them and bursts into laughter, interrupting the romantic encounter and bringing their secluded evening to an abrupt and embarrassing end.
outputs.L4:
In an idyllic pastoral setting, Silvia and Amyntas meet away from the eyes of the wider community. Amyntas is deeply attracted to Silvia, but his shyness makes every gesture of courtship uncertain. The poem’s playful narrator follows his awkward attempts to approach her, repeatedly punctuating the scene with the refrain “A ha ha ha ha.” The laughter is affectionate rather than cruel, emphasizing the comic distance between Amyntas’s strong desire and his limited courage.

Silvia gradually recognizes his intentions and responds with encouragement. Her willingness gives Amyntas the confidence to move closer, transforming his hesitation into a moment of mutual intimacy. At last, the pair are about to seal their courtship with a kiss, and the secrecy of their meeting seems to promise a brief escape from embarrassment and social scrutiny.

That privacy does not last. A passing shepherd unexpectedly discovers them and bursts into laughter, echoing the poem’s recurring refrain. His interruption turns the lovers’ tender moment into a public joke. The ending therefore combines romance with comedy: desire may be sincere, but it remains vulnerable to chance, exposure, and the amused gaze of others.
outputs.L5:
Evening settles softly over the world, painting the sky in shades of amber and violet. The day’s noise fades, and everything seems to breathe more slowly.

Beside you, love feels quiet—not a flame demanding to be seen, but a steady warmth, like lamplight in a familiar room. No words are needed. The calm between us says enough: we are here, the night is gentle, and for this moment, nothing is missing.

counterfactuals.output:
The lines are from the traditional broadside song **“William and Nancy”**, also catalogued under titles such as **“William and Nancy’s Parting”**. Broadside copies differ substantially, so I can’t reliably reproduce a complete text from the opening lines alone without risking combining variants.

The common opening stanza is:

> Calm was the evening, and clear was the sky,  
> And the new-budding flowers did spring;  
> The sun was gone down, and the shades drew around,  
> And the nightingale sweetly did sing.
